title: Political and Economic Changes and Development

guide.summary: Unit 5 examines how political and economic change interact: globalization and its effects, economic liberalization and privatization, resource dependence, social and demographic policy, and how governments in the course countries have responded to pressures for reform.

sections.heading: Economic models and liberalization
sections.body: Economic systems range from state-directed (command economies) to market-based. Many states adopted neoliberal reforms from the 1980s: privatization, deregulation, trade liberalization, reduced subsidies, often encouraged by the IMF and World Bank through structural adjustment. UK: Thatcher privatized state industries in the 1980s. Mexico: after import substitution industrialization (ISI) and the 1982 debt crisis, Mexico privatized firms, joined NAFTA (1994, replaced by USMCA in 2020), and in 2013 opened its energy sector to private investment; later governments moved to strengthen state firms like Pemex. China: Deng Xiaoping's reforms from 1978 introduced markets, special economic zones, and foreign investment while keeping one-party rule; China joined the WTO in 2001; the Belt and Road Initiative (2013) extends its influence abroad. Russia: rapid 1990s privatization ('shock therapy') created powerful oligarchs; Putin reasserted state control over strategic sectors such as energy.

sections.heading: Resources and globalization
sections.body: Rentier states depend on revenue from natural resources rather than taxation, which can reduce accountability. The resource curse links resource wealth to corruption, weak institutions, and conflict. Nigeria depends heavily on oil for government revenue and exports; oil price swings cause fiscal crises and the Niger Delta has seen conflict. Iran and Russia also rely on energy exports and face international sanctions. Globalization brings investment, trade, and growth but also inequality, loss of sovereignty, and backlash: Brexit (referendum 2016, exit 2020) reflected concerns about sovereignty and immigration. Supranational organizations (EU, WTO) require states to share some sovereignty.

sections.heading: Social and demographic policy
sections.body: Governments respond to demographic change. China's one-child policy (1980–2015) slowed population growth but contributed to aging and a gender imbalance; China moved to two children (2016) and three (2021). Russia faces population decline and offers 'maternity capital' payments for children. Iran promoted family planning in the late 1980s–1990s, then shifted toward pronatalist policies. Mexico's conditional cash transfer program (Progresa/Oportunidades/Prospera) paid poor families for school attendance and health visits; it was replaced in 2019 by direct transfers and scholarships. Nigeria's 2023 removal of the fuel subsidy saved revenue but raised prices sharply. Environmental policy: the UK's legally binding net zero target (2050) vs China's role as the largest emitter and largest producer of solar panels.

sections.heading: Applying it on the exam
sections.body: Comparative questions often ask how two countries responded to the same pressure. For globalization, compare China's state-led integration into world markets with Russia's reliance on energy exports. For social policy, compare Mexico's conditional cash transfers with China's population policies. Always name a specific policy, explain its purpose, and describe an effect on legitimacy, stability, or inequality.

sections.heading: Key terms
sections.body: Know neoliberalism, privatization, nationalization, import substitution industrialization, structural adjustment, rentier state, resource curse, foreign direct investment, supranational organization, and sovereignty.

sections.heading: Course-country examples
sections.body: UK: Thatcher-era privatization and Brexit. Mexico: NAFTA (1994), the 2013 energy reform, and conditional cash transfers. Nigeria: oil dependence, fuel subsidy removal in 2023, and the resource curse. Russia: 1990s privatization and oligarchs, later state control of energy, and sanctions. Iran: oil revenue, sanctions, and subsidies. China: Deng's reforms, WTO entry in 2001, and the Belt and Road Initiative. Use these to show how economic change affects political stability and legitimacy.

sections.heading: Linking economics and politics
sections.body: Economic performance affects legitimacy. When growth is strong, regimes like China's can claim performance legitimacy; when economies falter, governments face protests or electoral defeat. Inequality, corruption, and dependence on a single export increase instability. In comparative essays, show how a specific economic policy produced a political outcome, such as Mexico's economic liberalization contributing to the PRI's loss of dominance or Nigeria's oil dependence fueling corruption and regional conflict.

sections.heading: Exam tip
sections.body: Pair each policy with a specific year and an outcome, and when comparing countries, explain both a similarity and a difference. For example, China and Russia both moved away from command economies, but China kept one-party control while gradually liberalizing, whereas Russia's rapid shock therapy produced economic collapse and oligarchs.

keyTakeaways: Neoliberal reforms: privatization, deregulation, free trade.
China combined market reform with authoritarian rule.
Rentier states and the resource curse: Nigeria, Iran, Russia.
Demographic policies: one-child, maternity capital, cash transfers.
commonMistakes: Assuming economic liberalization always causes democratization (China).
Forgetting that NAFTA became USMCA in 2020.
Treating the resource curse as inevitable.
Ignoring the political motives behind economic policies.
examTips: Link economic policy to legitimacy (performance legitimacy in China).
Name a specific policy and year.
Explain both benefits and costs of globalization.
Compare policy responses across countries for Q3.

Describe a specific liberalizing policy in each of two course countries. C. Explain how each policy affected the government's legitimacy or political stability.

rubric.description: Reducing state control of the economy through privatization, deregulation, trade opening, or reduced subsidies.

1 point per accurate country policy (e.g., China SEZs/1978 reforms; Mexico NAFTA/privatization/2013 energy reform; Russia 1990s privatization; UK Thatcher privatization; Nigeria fuel subsidy removal).
1 point per explanation linking the policy to legitimacy or stability for that country.

practice.sampleResponse:
A. Economic liberalization means reducing the state's role in the economy, for example by privatizing state firms, lowering trade barriers, and removing price controls or subsidies.

B. China, beginning in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping, created special economic zones that welcomed foreign investment and allowed private enterprise. Russia in the early 1990s carried out rapid 'shock therapy' privatization of state-owned industries.

C. In China, decades of rapid growth from market reforms gave the Communist Party performance legitimacy, helping it maintain one-party rule without democratization. In Russia, rushed privatization concentrated wealth in a few oligarchs, contributed to economic collapse and inflation, and undermined trust in the new democratic institutions, which helped Putin later gain support by promising order and reasserting state control.
